Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator, in which Epic accuses Apple of narrowly interpreting its obligations under a recently reached App Store antitrust deal in Brazil. Here are the details.

A little background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it would now allow developers to distribute apps in Brazil through alternative app marketplaces.

The change was part of a settlement with Brazil that resolved a multi-year antitrust investigation. The investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. You can learn more about that structure here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to a report today from Brazil's O Globo (via MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE alleging that Apple has created "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic said that while Brazil's new terms only apply to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "expressly covers iPadOS."

Epic also reportedly objects to what it calls "scare screens" designed to discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store. It also criticizes the current installation flow, which it says requires nine steps, compared to Apple's current six-step implementation in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic added that Apple's initial installation flow in Europe required 15 steps, but after the company was ordered to reduce it to six, the "download abandonment rate fell from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is necessary to calculate fees" and allow the company "to monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
